Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- Humza Ismail hasn't spent much time in Raleigh, North Carolina, since he started graduate school two years ago. But when he heard two former acquaintances were arrested on terrorism charges this week, he says, "Honestly, I wasn't surprised." Omar Aly Hassan, left, and Ziyad Yaghi were clear on where they stood on terrorism, an acquaintance said. Omar Aly Hassan, Ziyad Yaghi and five others are charged with conspiring to commit violent jihad overseas. An eighth suspect is still being sought, authorities have said. When he lived in Raleigh, Ismail worshipped at the same mosque as Hassan and Yaghi. When groups of young men talked there, Ismail says, the conversation often turned to religion and politics, and Hassan and Yaghi made it clear where they stood. "When it came to something like suicide bombing, they would say, 'If it's a benefit for the Muslims then something like that can be permissible,' " Ismail says. "I could tell it was something they wanted to do." But, he adds, "They never indicated or said 'we are going to make jihad overseas.'" Ismail says the duo spoke in glowing terms about Osama bin Laden, calling him a scholar and a mujahedeen. "You could tell they were being influenced by somebody," Ismail says. He does not know by whom. He feels they were susceptible to a message of violence "because it sounded cool and exciting." Ismail says he strenuously disagreed with Yaghi and Hassan's views on terrorism even, he says, getting into a public shouting match with them at a restaurant. He says he told them, "You can't do this, man. You can't say it is OK. "That is corruption and terrorism and that is not permissible in Islam." Ismail says he and others raised concerns about Hassan and Yaghi to officials at the Islamic Center of Raleigh, but were "overlooked." "I did my part," Ismail says. Imran Aukhil, a spokesman for the Islamic Center of Raleigh, told CNN on Thursday that he had no information about complaints concerning Hassan and Yaghi. On Saturday, however, he informed CNN that he had researched the matter and learned there was a complaint several years ago against an individual at the mosque. Aukhil said he did not have the name of that person. "It was reported to the FBI," said Aukhil. "The FBI did take note of it in their investigation." Efforts to reach attorneys representing Hassan and Yaghi were unsuccessful.

outputs.L1:
**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Humza Ismail has not spent much time in Raleigh, North Carolina, since starting graduate school two years ago. But when he heard that two former acquaintances had been arrested on terrorism charges this week, he says, “Honestly, I wasn’t surprised.”

According to Ismail, Omar Aly Hassan and Ziyad Yaghi made their views on terrorism clear. Hassan, Yaghi and five others have been charged with conspiring to commit violent jihad overseas. Authorities say an eighth suspect is still being sought.

When he lived in Raleigh, Ismail worshipped at the same mosque as Hassan and Yaghi. He says that when groups of young men gathered there, their conversations often turned to religion and politics—and Hassan and Yaghi made their positions clear.

“When it came to something like suicide bombing, they would say, ‘If it’s a benefit for the Muslims, then something like that can be permissible,’” Ismail says. “I could tell it was something they wanted to do.”

However, he adds, “They never indicated or said, ‘We are going to make jihad overseas.’”

Ismail says the pair spoke glowingly of Osama bin Laden, describing him as a scholar and a mujahedeen.

“You could tell they were being influenced by somebody,” Ismail says, though he does not know by whom. He believes they were susceptible to a message of violence “because it sounded cool and exciting.”

Ismail says he strongly disagreed with Yaghi and Hassan’s views on terrorism, even becoming involved in a public shouting match with them at a restaurant.

He says he told them, “You can’t do this, man. You can’t say it is OK. That is corruption and terrorism, and that is not permissible in Islam.”

Ismail says he and others raised concerns about Hassan and Yaghi with officials at the Islamic Center of Raleigh, but their concerns were “overlooked.”

“I did my part,” Ismail says.

Imran Aukhil, a spokesman for the Islamic Center of Raleigh, told CNN on Thursday that he had no information about any complaints concerning Hassan and Yaghi. On Saturday, however, he informed CNN that he had researched the matter and learned that a complaint had been made several years ago against an individual at the mosque. Aukhil said he did not have that person’s name.

“It was reported to the FBI,” Aukhil said. “The FBI did take note of it in their investigation.”

Efforts to reach attorneys representing Hassan and Yaghi were unsuccessful.
outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — Since beginning graduate school two years ago, Humza Ismail has rarely been in Raleigh, North Carolina. Still, he said the arrests this week of two people he once knew on terrorism-related charges did not shock him.

“Honestly, I wasn’t surprised,” Ismail said.

Omar Aly Hassan and Ziyad Yaghi, along with five other people, have been accused of plotting to carry out violent jihad abroad. Authorities said an eighth suspect remains at large.

While living in Raleigh, Ismail attended the same mosque as Hassan and Yaghi. He said discussions among groups of young men there frequently shifted toward politics and religion, and the two men were open about their positions on terrorism.

According to Ismail, they would argue that suicide bombings could be allowed if they benefited Muslims. He said their comments gave him the impression that they were interested in taking such action. However, he added that neither man ever explicitly said they intended to wage jihad overseas.

Ismail also said Hassan and Yaghi praised Osama bin Laden, describing him as both a religious scholar and a mujahedeen. He believed someone was influencing them, though he did not know who. In his view, they were receptive to violent ideas because those ideas seemed exciting and appealing.

Ismail said he firmly opposed their beliefs about terrorism. At one point, he said, their disagreement escalated into a shouting argument in a restaurant. He recalled telling them they could not claim such conduct was acceptable because it amounted to corruption and terrorism and was forbidden under Islam.

He said he and other people alerted leaders at the Islamic Center of Raleigh about their concerns regarding Hassan and Yaghi, but those warnings were disregarded.

“I did my part,” Ismail said.

On Thursday, Islamic Center of Raleigh spokesman Imran Aukhil told CNN that he was unaware of any complaints involving Hassan and Yaghi. By Saturday, however, Aukhil said he had investigated further and discovered that a complaint had been filed several years earlier against someone at the mosque. He said he did not know that individual’s identity.

Aukhil said the matter had been reported to the FBI and that the agency had taken it into account during its investigation.

CNN’s attempts to contact lawyers for Hassan and Yaghi were unsuccessful.

According to the acquaintance, conversations with the two men frequently turned to Osama bin Laden, suicide bombings and armed jihad. He recalled Hassan and Yaghi praising bin Laden and defending suicide attacks as legitimate acts against perceived enemies of Islam. The acquaintance said he repeatedly challenged those views, arguing that the killing of civilians was incompatible with Islamic teachings and that their rhetoric was dangerous.

Concerned that the discussions reflected more than casual political anger, he said he brought the matter to officials at the Islamic Center of Raleigh. It is unclear what action, if any, mosque leaders took in response. His account raises questions about whether the men’s statements were recognized as warning signs and whether more could have been done to address their apparent radicalization.

Federal authorities later accused Hassan and Yaghi of participating in a conspiracy to travel abroad and wage violent jihad. The acquaintance’s recollections do not by themselves establish criminal conduct, and the allegations against the men remained subject to proof in court. Nevertheless, his description suggests that their increasingly extreme beliefs may have been visible within their local community before prosecutors intervened.

The account also illustrates the difficulty religious institutions face when members express radical ideas. Mosque leaders must distinguish between protected speech, provocative political opinions and genuine indications that someone may be moving toward violence. In this case, the former acquaintance believed the rhetoric had crossed a troubling line—and said he tried to ensure that community officials knew about it.

## Raleigh Jihad-Conspiracy Case: Militancy Allegations, Mosque Acquaintance’s Account, and Court Outcomes

### Overview

In July 2009, federal authorities announced charges against a group of North Carolina men accused of conspiring to support violent jihad and to carry out attacks overseas. Prosecutors portrayed the Raleigh-area network as a long-running conspiracy centered on Daniel Patrick Boyd, a convert to Islam who had previously traveled to Pakistan and Afghanistan.

The original indictment charged Boyd, two of his sons, and several associates with conspiring to provide material support to terrorists and conspiring to murder, kidnap, maim, or injure people abroad. An eighth suspect, Jude Kenan Mohammad, was initially charged as a fugitive. The case eventually produced guilty pleas and convictions, although not every allegation aired publicly—especially recollections about conversations at a mosque—was independently proved at trial.

### A former acquaintance’s description

A former mosque acquaintance offered one of the starkest personal accounts of the suspects’ alleged views. According to that acquaintance, members of the circle praised Osama bin Laden, regarded suicide bombing as religiously permissible, and displayed an attraction to violence that appeared driven partly by image and excitement.

The acquaintance recalled that the men spoke approvingly of bin Laden and said they considered suicide bombing permissible. In describing their apparent fascination with militancy, the acquaintance said violence seemed “cool and exciting” to them.

That account was significant because it suggested the alleged radicalization was visible in informal discussions before the arrests. It also presented the group’s attraction to jihadism as a mixture of ideology, admiration for prominent extremists, and the allure of danger.

At the same time, the remarks should be understood for what they were: one former acquaintance’s recollections. Statements to journalists or investigators can provide context, but they are not equivalent to judicial findings. The government’s case rested on evidence presented through indictments, testimony, recorded statements, travel preparations, weapons activity, and the defendants’ own pleas or trial records.

### The defendants and alleged conspiracy

The principal defendant was Daniel Patrick Boyd, who lived in the Raleigh area and operated a drywall business. Federal prosecutors alleged that Boyd had received military-style training in Pakistan and Afghanistan between 1989 and 1992 and later used his experience to encourage others to pursue violent jihad.

The original defendants included:

- Daniel Patrick Boyd  
- His sons Dylan Boyd and Zakariya Boyd  
- Hysen Sherifi  
- Anes Subasic  
- Ziyad Yaghi  
- Mohammad Omar Aly Hassan  
- Jude Kenan Mohammad, who was initially a fugitive  

Prosecutors alleged that members of the group trained with firearms, discussed violent jihad, recruited others, raised or supplied money, and traveled or attempted to travel abroad in search of opportunities to fight. The government cited destinations including Israel, Jordan, Kosovo, and Pakistan.

The case was principally about an alleged conspiracy to commit violence outside the United States. Prosecutors did not initially accuse the men of having selected a specific civilian target in Raleigh or of being on the verge of carrying out a domestic bombing.

### Boyd’s alleged leadership role

Authorities described Daniel Boyd as the central organizer and ideological influence. The indictment alleged that he promoted violent jihad as a religious obligation and helped members of the group prepare for possible combat.

Boyd’s overseas history was an important part of the prosecution narrative. He had traveled to South Asia when the war against Soviet forces in Afghanistan still shaped international jihadist movements. Prosecutors maintained that this earlier experience gave him credibility with younger associates and enabled him to present himself as someone familiar with armed struggle.

The defense and some people who knew Boyd disputed the government’s characterization of him. Supporters described him as a family man and questioned whether religious discussions, firearm use, and international travel had been interpreted in the most incriminating possible way. The case therefore raised recurring questions about where protected beliefs and associations end and criminal preparation begins.

### Weapons, travel, and alleged preparation

The government argued that the conspiracy went beyond rhetoric. Among other things, prosecutors pointed to:

- Firearms possession and training  
- Discussions about traveling to conflict zones  
- Attempts by some defendants to travel abroad  
- Alleged recruitment of additional participants  
- Financial or logistical assistance  
- Statements endorsing violent jihad  

These allegations mattered because expressions of radical or offensive beliefs are generally protected by the First Amendment. To obtain convictions, prosecutors needed evidence of agreements, actions, or knowing assistance connected to unlawful violence—not merely proof that defendants held extremist opinions.

The former acquaintance’s statements about praise for bin Laden, approval of suicide bombing, and an attraction to what seemed “cool and exciting” supplied background about the group’s alleged outlook. They did not, by themselves, establish the charged conspiracies.

### Guilty pleas and trial results

The case did not end with a single collective verdict. Several defendants pleaded guilty, while others went to trial.

Daniel Boyd ultimately pleaded guilty to conspiracy charges and cooperated with federal authorities. His sons also entered guilty pleas. In 2011, a federal jury convicted Hysen Sherifi, Ziyad Yaghi, and Anes Subasic of terrorism-related conspiracy offenses. The resulting sentences varied according to each defendant’s conduct, charges, plea agreements, and cooperation.

Sherifi later faced additional charges arising from a separate alleged plot to kill government witnesses and people involved in the original prosecution. That later case reinforced the government’s portrayal of him as committed to retaliatory violence, but it was legally distinct from the initial overseas-jihad conspiracy.

### Jude Kenan Mohammad

Jude Kenan Mohammad remained outside the United States after being charged. He was later reported killed in Pakistan in a U.S. drone strike. Because he was never brought back for trial, the allegations against him in the Raleigh indictment were not adjudicated through a U.S. criminal verdict.

### Significance of the case

The Raleigh prosecution became an important example of the federal government’s post-September 11 approach to preventive terrorism cases. Rather than waiting for a completed attack, authorities used conspiracy and material-support laws to intervene when they believed a group had moved from extremist advocacy toward preparation and assistance.

The case also illustrated the evidentiary and civil-liberties tensions inherent in such prosecutions. Religious discussion, political anger, international travel, and lawful gun ownership can each be innocent or constitutionally protected. Prosecutors therefore sought to show that, taken together with recruitment efforts, travel plans, training, and agreements to participate in violence, those activities formed part of a criminal conspiracy.

The former mosque acquaintance’s account gave the public a vivid window into the attitudes allegedly circulating within the group. Praise for bin Laden and acceptance of suicide bombing suggested ideological sympathy with extremist violence, while the description of militancy as “cool and exciting” pointed to a more personal and psychological attraction. Yet the legal case ultimately depended not on how disturbing those views sounded, but on whether prosecutors could prove that individual defendants knowingly agreed to support or participate in unlawful violence.

### Conclusion

The Raleigh jihad-conspiracy case combined radical ideology, overseas ambitions, family and mosque relationships, firearms activity, and federal preventive enforcement. The former acquaintance’s recollections portrayed suspects who praised bin Laden, considered suicide bombing permissible, and appeared drawn to violence because it seemed “cool and exciting.” Those recollections helped explain why people around the group may have regarded its conversations as alarming.

The convictions and guilty pleas, however, rested on the broader body of evidence developed by investigators and tested through the judicial process. Careful reporting should therefore distinguish among allegations in the indictment, a witness or acquaintance’s personal recollections, facts admitted in guilty pleas, and conduct established by jury verdicts.
